newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WEEK AHEAD-Rate outlook to dominate Australia markets.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Rate outlook to dominate Australia markets.

text.p: The interest rate outlook is likely to be the dominant force on Australian markets this week, culminating on Thursday when the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) governor speaks and key employment data are released.

The RBA Board meets on Tuesday but despite continued labour market weakness last week's stronger than expected wages data has seen essentially all expectations of Governor Ian Macfarlane making an announcement at 9.30 a.m (2330 GMT) on Wednesday disappear.
"Markets now appear to accept the view that the RBA is unlikely to seriously canvass any change in the immediate term," Macquarie Bank economists said.
But while no one expects to hear from Macfarlane on Wednesday morning, plenty is expected from him on Thursday.
Macfarlane will be making the first semi-annual report on the conduct of monetary policy to the House of Representatives Standing Committee on Financial Institutions and Public Administration.
He will make a report to the committee, and then take questions. Some of those questions are expected to centre on the high unemployment rate, and whether the bank can do more to reduce it.

"The big question they will all want to ask is why the Bank does not cut rates, when unemployment is so high, employment growth so slow, and inflation so slight," HSBC Markets chief economist John Edwards said.
"It is not an easy question to answer."
Analysts say Macfarlane can use the pace of wages growth as a reason why the RBA has not eased, assuming no move follows Tuesday's board meeting.
But against that, unemployment remains above 8.5 percent, and there has been some tempering of the strength seen in some indicators earlier in the year.
And Macfarlane is not expected to get any help from April labour force data released while he is before the committee.
Economists expect that while employment will rise by around 35,000 as a correction to the weakness of February and March, the unemployment rate will remain steady at 8.7 percent.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (Friday: 10-year bond yield 7.86 pct, -0.08)

The bond market should start the week with a stronger bias following Friday's U.S. led gains on the favourable reaction to the key non-farm payrolls report, and news of a U.S. balanced budget accord was also supportive for the Treasury market.

Locally the Reserve Bank board meeting on Tuesday is not expected to produce any change in policy, although traders will still be watching the central bank's dealing screens on Wednesday on the slimest off chances of an announcement.

However, last week's strong rise in first quarter wages growth to an annual rate of 4.6 percent, and above the RBA's 4.5 percent "line in the sand", has all but killed off speculation of any easing this month.

"We suspect that events next week will do little to dent the negative sentiment that emerged following the higher than expected earnings data ... and the strong Q1 GDP result indicated by the retail trade data," said Commonwealth Bank of Australia in its weekly review.

On the data side, the market faces the Australian labour force report for April on Thursday with the unemployment rate keenly watched for any improvement, although economists expect its to stay at 8.7 percent, which may keep open the option of a policy easing further down the track.
For the semi government market, the NSW state Budget will be released on Tuesday afternoon.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri: US$0.7731/36, New York US$0.7827/32)
The troubles of the debt market last week were salve to the dollar which saw its yield advantage over the U.S. dollar restored and increased across the curve.
This attracted demand from offshore investors, particularly Japan where rates still remain near record lows.

They were seen buying A$ government bonds direct and the flow of yen/A$ dual currency samurai bonds started up again after dying away in recent months. There was talk of more of these in the pipeline for this week which should keep the dollar underpinned near last week's five year high of 100.00 yen.
Dealers also detected good support around US$0.7820 and expected it to grind past US$0.7860 this week (depending on what the U.S. payrolls do to U.S. rate expectations).

The main events of the week -- assuming the RBA board meeting stays pat as expected -- should be governor Ian Macfarlane's testimony on monetary policy to a Parliamentary committee and the employment data on Thursday.
A weak jobs number would increase pressure for an easing and could see the dollar test US$0.7785 again if Macfarlane did not explicitly rule out a cut.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS (Fri: All Ords Index 2,491.6, +6.2)
Wall Street has set a positive tone for the start to the week after a strong Friday saw the Dow post its largest weekly points gain on record.
The local market had proved itself to be well supported last week despite failing to hold the desirable territory above 2,500, a level it may reclaim if the market follows the U.S. lead.

While the positive bias from the U.S. will help, local players were now much more focussed on local fundamentals with the change in tack meaning major moves in the U.S. were being less and less reflected locally.
"Our market hasn't gone crazy at any time and there is enough in the market to keep it interesting," said Andrew Sekely, head of equities at Intersuisse.
Investors were likely to continue to be choosy, with buying centred on the leaders rather than widespread interest.
Corporate news remained thin on the ground with grocer Foodland third quarter sales on Thursday the pick.
Annual meetings include insurer HIH Winterthur International Holdings on Friday.

In economic data terms, the local labour force figures for April, due on Thursday, will be keenly watched to discern any effect on interest rate expectations, as will Macfarlane's appearance on the same day.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
